column2: When the demons' strength grew, the defeated denizens of heaven abandoned the world of the gods and fled in fear.
Disguised in human forms, they wandered over the earth, while Bali, son of Virochana, devoted to Narayana, enjoyed the three worlds.
With unobstructed lordship and flourishing prosperity, that mighty one sacrificed with horse-sacrifices, intent on pleasing Vishnu.
He also held the offices of Indra in heaven and of the guardians of the quarters; in all those sacrifices that Brahmins perform to please the gods,
the king of the demons consumed the offerings. Aditi, mother of the gods, seeing her sons so, was greatly grieved.
Intent on meditating on Hari, she performed very hard austerity: for a while sitting, then standing,
for long on one foot, then on the tips of her toes; for a time eating fruit, then eating fallen leaves,
then living on water, then on air, then abstaining from all food, meditating by herself on the Self, a mass of being-consciousness-bliss.
For a thousand divine years she practised that austerity, O Narada. Hearing of her unending austerity, the deceitful demons, urged on by Bali,
took the forms of gods and said to Aditi: "Mother, why do you torment yourself and dry up your body?
If the demons learn of it, there will be great sorrow; give up this painful drying of the body.
The wise do not praise merit that must be won by toil; the body is to be guarded with effort by those intent on the means of dharma.
Those who neglect the body are self-destroyers. Live happily, good lady, and do not trouble us, your sons.
People without a mother, mother, are nearly dead, without doubt; cows or animals, even trees —
those without a mother find no happiness and are like the dead. A poor man, a sick man, one gone to another land,
gains the highest joy by merely seeing his mother. In food, in water, in wealth or among loved ones,
no one ever turns away from his mother. He whose house has no mother, no devoted woman faithful to dharma and loving her husband, should go to the forest.
Dharma is empty without devotion to Narayana; wealth without good enjoyment; a house without a wife and children: so is a man without a mother.
Therefore, goddess, save your sons who are in distress." Though thus addressed by the demons, Aditi did not stir from her meditation.
Having said this, all the demons, seeing her intent on meditating on Hari, became angry and plotted to kill her.
Roaring like clouds at the end of an age, their eyes red with rage, they released fire from the tips of their tusks; it burned the forest in a moment.
The forest, a hundred yojanas wide and full of creatures, was burned, and the demons who had gone to attack her were burned by that same fire.
But the mother of the gods remained, her mind fixed on Achyuta for a hundred years, protected by Vishnu's discus Sudarshana, the demon-slayer, compassionate to his own.
O best of demons, from these wives he had two hundred and forty sons, all perpetually hungry.
Penniless, Bhadramati, seeing his beloved sons tormented by hunger and being hungry himself, lamented, his senses distraught:

Cursed is a birth without fortune, cursed a birth without wealth; cursed a birth without dharma, cursed a birth without fame.
naradapuran:10:145	Cursed is the birth of a man with many children and without prosperity. Ah, good qualities, gentleness, learning, birth in a good family —
naradapuran:10:146	to one sunk in the ocean of poverty, all this does not shine. Dear sons, grandsons, kinsmen, brothers,
naradapuran:10:147	disciples and all people abandon one without wealth. A Chandala or a Brahmin, only the fortunate man is honoured.
naradapuran:10:148	A poor man in the world is despised like a corpse. Ah, one joined with riches, though harsh, is called gentle;
naradapuran:10:149	though without virtue, he is called virtuous; fool or scholar, if he has wealth he is honoured, without doubt.
naradapuran:10:150	Ah, poverty is sorrow, and in it hope gives the greatest sorrow; men overcome by hope suffer imperishable pain.
naradapuran:10:151	Those who are slaves to hope are slaves to the whole world; those for whom hope is a slave, the world serves.
naradapuran:10:152	Honour is the imperishable wealth of the great in the world; when honour, with hope as its enemy, is lost, poverty comes.
naradapuran:10:153	Even one who knows the meaning of all scriptures looks like a fool when poor. Who can free those seized by the great crocodile of destitution?
naradapuran:10:154	Ah, sorrow! Ah, sorrow! Ah, sorrow — poverty! And in it the multitude of sons and wives gives the greatest sorrow.
Having said this, Bhadramati, who had mastered the meaning of all scriptures, then pondered another dharma that gives prosperity.
Deciding on the gift of land, the best of all gifts — he who approves of giving did this in the past —
the supreme dharma that attains and grants the fruit of all desires; of gifts, the gift of land is declared the best.
By giving it a man gains whatever he most desires. Having resolved thus, the wise Bhadramati, O Bali,
went with his wife and children to the city named Kaushambi, to the best of Brahmins named Sughosha, who had every prosperity.
Going there, O Bali, he begged a piece of land five cubits long. Sughosha, devoted to dharma, seeing that householder,
with a pleased mind honoured him and said: "I am fulfilled, Bhadramati, and my birth is fruitful.
My family has been purified by your favour, O Brahmin." Having said so and honoured him, Sughosha, devoted to dharma,
the greatly wise one gave him land five cubits in measure with the verse: "The earth is Vishnu's, holy; the earth is protected by Vishnu;
by the gift of the earth may Janardana be pleased with me." With this mantra, O king of demons, Sughosha,
honouring that best of Brahmins as Vishnu, gave that much land. And Bhadramati the Brahmin, the wise,
gave the land he had begged to a householder, a Vedic scholar and devotee of Hari. By the gift of land Sughosha, with ten million generations of his family,
reached Vishnu's abode, from which one does not grieve. And Bhadramati too, O Bali, since he had asked for prosperity,
stayed with his family in Vishnu's abode for ten thousand ages, and likewise in Brahma's abode for ten million ages,
then attained Indra's station for five kalpas; afterward, reaching earth with all prosperity,
the greatly fortunate one enjoyed excellent pleasures, remembering his past births. Then, O demon, Bhadramati, free of desire and devoted to Vishnu,
gave the earth to Brahmins without livelihood. Pleased, Vishnu gave him the unsurpassed lordship of the truth,
and, with ten million generations of his family, unsurpassed liberation. Therefore, O lord of demons, devoted to all dharma,
I shall practise austerity for liberation; give me land of three steps." Then Bali, son of Virochana, saw a vessel filled with water
and took it to give the earth to the dwarf Vamana, wearing the student's garb. Vishnu, all-pervading, knowing that Shukra was blocking the flow of water,
placed the tip of the kusha grass he held into the water-spout. At the grass tip there arose a great weapon, bright as ten million suns,
unfailing, most fierce, eager to destroy Shukra's eye. Shukra came to the demons with one eye.
Look! he ordered; the kusha tip was like a weapon. Bali gave Mahavishnu the earth of three steps.
Then the Soul of the universe grew until he reached Brahma's world; Hari, whose body is the universe, measured the earth with two steps.
His steps reached from the earth to the roof of the cosmic egg; the tip of his toe pierced the egg and split it in two.
Through that opening, water from outside came in many streams: the pure water, which had washed Vishnu's foot, purifier of the worlds.
Dwelling outside the egg of Brahma, it took the form of a stream; that best purifying water purified Brahma and the gods,
and, served by the seven sages, fell on the peak of Meru.
Seeing that wonderful deed, Brahma and the hosts of gods, the sages and Manus praised him, overcome with joy.

The gods said: "Homage to the Supreme Lord, whose form is the Supreme Self, higher than the highest, who bears lower forms, whose Self is Brahman, whose mind delights in Brahman, who is of unobstructed action.
O Supreme Lord, supreme bliss, Supreme Self, higher than the highest, Self of all, whose form is the world, beyond proof — homage to you.
Homage to you who have eyes everywhere, arms everywhere, heads everywhere, and a course everywhere."
Thus praised by Brahma and the other dwellers of heaven, the eternal God of gods rejoiced, granting fearlessness.
He bound the demon son of Virochana for lack of a third step. Then, knowing Bali had taken refuge, he gave him Rasatala and became his doorkeeper, bound by his devotee.
Narada said: In Rasatala, terrible and full of the fear of serpents, what food did Mahavishnu provide for the son of Virochana?
Sanaka said: An offering made without invitation, one poured into the fire, and what is given to an unworthy recipient — these become terrible means of enjoyment there.
An offering made by an impure person, a rite done with pride — all of that there is fit to be enjoyed, and gives the fruit of a fall below.
So Vishnu gave Rasatala to Bali with his demons, and gave the three heavens to all the gods, granting fearlessness.
Worshipped by the hosts of immortals, praised by great sages, sung by Gandharvas, he again took the form of the dwarf.
